title: FACT CHECK: Marcoleta plunder case has not been dismissed
summary: In a November 23 ruling, the Sandiganbayan denied Marcoleta’s bail petition, with the court finding strong evidence of guilt against him — the threshold of evidence required for bail petitions

blocks.text: Claim: The plunder case against Senator Rodante Marcoleta has been dismissed.

Why we fact-checked this: A reel posted on November 18 by the Facebook page Norbel Vidal shows Marcoleta standing at a lectern, with the text, “Demurrer to Evidence — tapos na ang kaso. Dismissed agad!”
(Demurrer to Evidence — the case is over. Dismissed immediately!)
Additional text overlaid on the reel hints at Marcoleta’s supposed return to office now that the case against him has been junked.

Several social media users welcomed the alleged development in the senator’s case, with some expressing their support for Marcoleta. As of writing, the post has garnered over 148,000 views, 4,200 reactions, 210 comments, and 369 shares.
The facts: There is no court ruling, official statement, or credible report showing that Marcoleta’s case has been dismissed.

The reel was referring to a legal move by Marcoleta and his three co-accused — former lawmaker Michael Defensor and businessmen Aristotle Viray and Joseph Espiritu — who are seeking the dismissal of the P75-million plunder case against them.
On November 11, Sandiganbayan 3rd Division Clerk of Court Dennis Pulma confirmed that Marcoleta and his co-accused had filed motions for leave to file a demurrer to evidence.
A demurrer to evidence asks a court to dismiss a case on the ground that the prosecution’s evidence is insufficient to establish guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
The misleading reel, however, frames Marcoleta’s legal move as though the court had already ruled to dismiss the plunder case.

Contrary to the claim, the senator’s case remains active. On November 23, the anti-graft court’s 3rd Division denied Marcoleta’s petition for bail, ruling that the evidence of guilt against him is strong — the threshold of evidence required for bail petitions.
This ruling, however, is not a guilty verdict against Marcoleta and his co-accused.

Marcoleta’s plunder case: The case against the lawmaker concerns P75 million in campaign donations Marcoleta received for his 2025 senatorial run, which the Ombudsman says he failed to declare in his Statement of Contributions and Expenditures and his Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth. (READ: How Marcoleta spent P112.9 million in his 2025 election campaign)
Marcoleta has rejected the allegations against him, arguing that they had no legal basis or merit.

The lawmaker has been suspended as a senator since October 19. He has been detained since July after surrendering to authorities following the issuance of a warrant for his arrest on plunder charges filed by the Office of the Ombudsman.
Aside from plunder, Marcoleta is also facing three counts of alleged violation of Presidential Decree No. 46 (receiving gifts).
